transcript:
[00:00] Lara Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Lara from Redwood. We have about 45 minutes, I know you have a busy week, so we'll keep it tight. Devon, do you want to intro?
[00:08] Devon Patel: Yeah hi, I'm Devon on the engineering side — I mainly help with private and dedicated installs. Today we want to understand Helio's constraints for a private or air‑gapped deployment.
[00:18] Aisha Rahman: Thanks. Quick context: Helio supports clinical decision support, so we need HIPAA controls, some FIPS requirements for crypto, and several sites are completely isolated — no outbound internet.
[00:28] Tom Willis: Also, hardware note: we have mixed GPU inventory across two datacenters — some A100s, a small H100 pool arriving next quarter, and a bunch of older 32GB cards. We can't guarantee NVLink across clusters.
[00:38] Devon Patel: Got it. So the two main constraints I'm hearing are network isolation (no egress) and heterogeneous GPU hardware. Also you mentioned FIPS — KMS posture matters.
[00:47] Priya Desai: Right, and one more — all updates must be reviewed and pushed via our internal change control. We can't accept outbound pull from a vendor.
[00:55] Lara Kim: That's the common air‑gap pattern — customers want either a vendor-signed offline package or a site-to-site secure transfer. We'll talk options: full Private (Redwood-managed control plane inside your VPC) vs an on‑prem air‑gapped bundle that you run yourself.
[01:05] Aisha Rahman: We're mostly leaning toward the air‑gapped bundle. We want to avoid vendor agents that phone home.
[01:12] Devon Patel: Understood. For the bundle approach we provide: container images tarball, orchestration manifests (K8s or systemd), model artifacts in quantized format if desired, and an offline installer script. The installer can run against an internal update server — or via USB if required.
[01:28] Tom Willis: USB is fine for one-off updates, but for regular security patches we want an internal staging server that ingests signed artifacts. How do you sign and verify artifacts?
[01:36] Devon Patel: We sign release artifacts with a GPG/PKI chain and provide checksums and signature verification steps. We can also provide an HSM-backed signing key or work with your KMS to verify signatures locally.
[01:45] Priya Desai: Do you support FIPS-validated crypto stacks? That's a blocker for some customers.
[01:51] Devon Patel: We don't ship a FIPS module by default in the bundle but we can provide a FIPS-compatible build or guidance to link against your FIPS module. We'll need to scope that with your security team; it's typically a small engineering effort but important to validate.
[02:02] Lara Kim: Also, operationally — if you want Redwood to manage the control plane but isolate it to your VPC, that's our Private offering. That requires some egress for telemetry unless you opt into full offline logs collection. We can discuss options.
[02:15] Aisha Rahman: For compliance, we prefer zero egress. Is there a supported mode where Redwood only provides the software and we manage everything — no telemetry?
[02:24] Devon Patel: Yes, the 'air‑gapped bundle' is exactly that: we produce artifacts and docs; you run everything. We provide an enterprise support SLA with runbooks. We also offer an 'observer mode' where logs are stored locally and support access is via customer-provided jumpbox or temporary bastion with audited sessions.
[02:40] Tom Willis: About hardware: with mixed GPU types, how tolerant is Redwood's runtime? Can you do model routing based on device capability?
[02:48] Devon Patel: The runtime supports model variants and quantization; you can pin a model to specific node labels. For example, route heavy models to H100s and smaller ones to A100s or quantized variants. If you have 32GB cards we may suggest tensor-sliced configurations or lower batch sizes.
[03:01] Aisha Rahman: What's the expected performance delta for quantized models? Our clinical checks are latency sensitive.
[03:08] Devon Patel: Typically 8-bit quantization gives 1.5–3x throughput improvement and modest latency change per token; for strict p50 latency SLOs we test on your representative prompt set. We always recommend a small benchmark against your workload.
[03:21] Lara Kim: We'll propose a pilot: a short benchmark run using a sanitized prompt set in your environment. That way we can size and recommend quantization profiles.
[03:29] Tom Willis: On the patching cadence — if we accept offline bundles, how do you handle CVEs and critical updates? We need a process for expedited patches.
[03:37] Devon Patel: We have an expedited patch pipeline: Redwood creates an emergency bundle, signs it, and we can coordinate a secure transfer. We also provide a recommended checklist for testing and rollback procedures.
[03:47] Priya Desai: On certs and KMS — can Redwood integrate with our on‑prem HSM (Thales)?
[03:52] Devon Patel: Yes, we have customers using PKCS#11 HSMs and can support key material being managed by your HSM. We'll need to validate APIs and may require a small adapter if anything is proprietary.
[04:03] Aisha Rahman: Licensing/cost — how does pricing work when we're fully on‑premocratic? (laughs) I mean, fully on‑prem.
[04:10] Lara Kim: For air‑gapped bundles we typically do an enterprise license: upfront platform fee + annual support. If you want Redwood to run Dedicated capacity in your datacenter we can do reserved capacity pricing. We'll share a pricing sheet but pricing varies with support level and private management.
[04:24] Tom Willis: What about SLA — if we run it ourselves, what's the response time?
[04:28] Lara Kim: Our support tiers include four‑hour for critical incidents, 24x7 for certain tiers. For self-managed installs we add runbook enablement and on‑call escalation paths.
[04:36] Devon Patel: I want to clarify one technical nit: when you said "no Kubernetes" earlier, do you mean you don't run any K8s at all, or you prefer not to depend on it?
[04:44] Tom Willis: We don't have a cluster we can use for this. We run VMs and Nomad in one site. We could spin up a small K8s cluster but it's not trivial.
[04:52] Devon Patel: Okay — we can provide a systemd/systemctl installer path instead of a k8s chart. It's slightly less automated but works fine for single-node or small clusters.
[05:00] Priya Desai: Another compliance question: audit logs retention. We need immutable logs for 2 years and tamper evidence.
[05:07] Devon Patel: Logs are shipped to your local logging cluster — we support append-only write paths and can integrate with your WORM storage for long retention. We'll include log hashing and signed checkpoints as part of the bundle.
[05:18] Aisha Rahman: Great. Any red flags you see on our side?
[05:21] Devon Patel: The main thing is the hardware mismatch and the isolated update process — both solvable but we need inventory and acceptance tests. Also planning for the H100 arrival timeline matters to decide whether to build now or plan a phased rollout.
[05:32] Lara Kim: Recap / next steps: we'll send SOC2 + FIPS notes, a private deployment checklist, and an offline installer artifact as a demo. We'll request Tom's hardware inventory and a sanitized prompt set for benchmarking.
[05:44] Tom Willis: Sounds good. We can provide rack specs by Wednesday.
[05:47] Priya Desai: I want to schedule the deep dive with Devon to go through HSM and FIPS needs — prefer next week.
[05:53] Lara Kim: I'll propose times. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the package and suggested dates.
[05:58] Aisha Rahman: Thanks. One quick Q: you mentioned model rollbacks — what does that look like in the air‑gapped install?
[06:04] Devon Patel: Rollbacks are supported via versioned artifacts — the installer keeps previous model bundles and the runtime can pin to a previous SHA. We'll document the rollback playbook.
[06:14] Lara Kim: Ok we'll include that in the runbook. Any final quick items?
[06:18] Tom Willis: No. Thanks.
[06:19] Lara Kim: Great, bye everyone.
